title: Agentic AI system design readiness check

items.stem: Which feature most clearly separates an agent from a single model call?

options.text: It uses a large model that follows complex, multi-part instructions reliably.
It has access to several tools, even if each request calls only one.
It loops: it chooses an action, observes the result and decides again until a stop condition.
It returns structured JSON that downstream code can parse and act on.

items.stem: A system sends every document to a model once to extract a date, then stores it. What is it?

options.text: A fixed pipeline step.
An agent.
A planner and executor.
A multi-agent system.

items.stem: When deciding how much autonomy to give a model, what is the safest default?

options.text: Maximum autonomy, so it can handle any case.
Whatever level the chosen framework provides.
A level the model chooses for itself at run time.
The lowest level of autonomy that meets the requirement.

items.stem: A model emits a tool call to delete a customer record. What should happen next?

options.text: The record is deleted immediately, since the model asked for it.
The orchestrator decides whether to act, and the tool gateway checks permission before anything executes.
The model is asked to confirm its own call, then the record is deleted.
The call is logged and executed in parallel with the next model step.

items.stem: Each step of a 10-step agent succeeds 98 per cent of the time, independently. Roughly how often does the whole run succeed?

options.text: About 98 per cent.
About 90 per cent.
About 82 per cent.
About 50 per cent.

items.stem: A search tool returns HTTP 200 with no results for a valid query. How should the system represent that?

options.text: As a distinct EMPTY result that the model can reason about.
As SUCCESS with an empty string, since the HTTP call itself worked.
As UNAVAILABLE, so the orchestrator retries the search with backoff.
As an exception that ends the run.

items.stem: An agent keeps calling the same search with exactly the same arguments. Which safeguard targets this most directly?

options.text: A larger context window.
A higher sampling temperature.
A higher step ceiling.
A no-progress detector.

items.stem: Which statement of requirements lets you rule a design in or out before building it?

options.text: It must be fast and cheap.
Under 20 seconds at p95 and $0.02 per task, at 40,000 tasks a day.
It must beat the current system.
It must be scalable and reliable.

items.stem: Tasks arrive at 4 per second at peak, and each takes 5 seconds on average. How many tasks are in flight at peak?
Your model provider starts rate-limiting requests at peak. Which response best fits a degradation ladder?

options.text: Route to a smaller standby model with shorter output, and tell users answers are briefer for now.
Show an error page with a retry button until the provider fully recovers.
Retry every rate-limited request with backoff until each one succeeds.
Keep the primary model but quietly truncate prompts so requests cost less.

items.stem: Why should a tool gateway authorise the caller before validating the arguments?

options.text: Authorisation is cheaper, so running it first saves latency on every call.
It lets the model retry with corrected arguments once access is granted.
The order does not matter, provided both checks run before execution.
So a denied caller never learns the tool's schema from validation errors.

items.stem: Steps succeed 0.99 of the time, independently. What is the most steps a run can have while keeping end-to-end success at or above 0.90?
